data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A trained non-expert panel will NOT, on average, produce more reliable judgments than a single domain expert, because the panel's reliance on an explicit checklist transfers the locus of judgment from the evaluator to the checklist designer, meaning the panel's output is a measure of the checklist's quality, not the panel's reliability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the panel's aggregate judgment consistently outperforms the checklist's literal output (e.g., by averaging out checklist biases), the panel itself is contributing reliability beyond the checklist.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If domain expertise is primarily about avoiding known pitfalls rather than integrating complex novel information, a checklist encoding those pitfalls will outperform intuition.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert's intuition is subject to systemic biases (e.g., anchoring) that the checklist disrupts, the checklist's objectivity is a genuine reliability gain.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The expert's intuition is a highly compressed, implicitly validated model of the domain. A non-expert panel using a checklist is merely a distributed execution engine for an externalized model. If the checklist is perfect, the panel is reliable, but this is an artifact of the checklist, not the panel. Genuine reliability gain requires the panel to process information better than the expert, which an explicit checklist does not facilitate; it only enforces compliance.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
